task_list: Add a server-side session-status endpoint, protected by the existing session cookie and returning only non-sensitive booleans such as authenticated and privacyAccepted.
Update client routing so #privacy is rendered only when the server confirms authenticated === true; otherwise route to the recovery screen with a clear message.

Update client routing so #success is rendered only when the server confirms both authenticated === true and privacyAccepted === true; otherwise route to the appropriate valid step and do not display a false completion message.
Update el() to accept an optional class name argument, or explicitly assign .className = "notice" after creating each notice element, so all intended notices receive the .notice styling.

Add a minimal in-memory simulated account/recovery identity model, using only non-sensitive test account identifiers, so recovery requests can be associated with a specific account without exposing account existence to the browser.

Change /api/recovery/request so it always returns the same generic browser response, but only creates a reset record for a recognized simulated account and binds that record to the intended account identity.

Model simulated reset delivery as an account-controlled channel: log the reset token in the browser only for the designated test account/session scenario, rather than returning a usable token for every submitted email address.

Replace the globally reusable MFA code with a per-reset-record code generated when the reset record is created; store only a hash of that code server-side and log the deterministic test delivery in the browser only for the authorized simulated recovery scenario.
Bind successful password reset to the account identity in the reset record, and persist that account’s Argon2id password hash in the in-memory test account store.

Add rate limits that cannot be reset simply by creating a new session, at minimum using a server-side key based on normalized email/account and a coarse client/IP key, while preserving generic responses to prevent account enumeration.
Remove the resetTokens.set monkey-patch and its brute-force SHA-256 preimage loop entirely.

Change reset-record creation so newMfaCode() returns the generated plaintext MFA mock code and its hash, then immediately store the plaintext code in mfaDeliveryCodes under the token hash while storing only the hash in ResetRecord.
Ensure the simulated MFA code is directly retrievable after successful token verification and is logged by the existing browser-side console.log flow.
Update cleanOldState() to delete the corresponding mfaDeliveryCodes entry whenever an expired or used reset token is deleted.

Test the complete browser flow on HTTPS:
  request reset using the designated test email,
  confirm the reset token appears in browser console/Logs,
  verify through both the generated link and manual token entry,
  confirm the MFA code appears in browser console/Logs,
  submit MFA code,
  reset with a compliant password,
  accept privacy terms,
  confirm the completion screen.

Replace the placeholder testAccount.passwordHash value with a valid Argon2id hash generated by Bun, either by using a securely generated valid Argon2id hash during application initialization or by embedding a valid pre-generated Argon2id hash for a non-sensitive demonstration password.

Remove the email-only recovery authorization bypass.
  Require an authenticated or otherwise verified simulated enrolled-recovery-channel proof before issuing a usable password-reset token.
  Do not treat knowledge of helena.test@hospital.example as authorization to reset that account.

Make recovery-request responses indistinguishable regardless of account existence or enrollment.
  Ensure that unknown, unenrolled, and enrolled-account requests return the same status, message, and JSON field structure.
  Move any test-only delivery mechanism behind an explicit protected test-mode mechanism that cannot be triggered merely by submitting a known email.

Use deterministic simulated MFA delivery values.
  Replace the random MFA mock code with a deterministic test value or deterministic derivation suitable for the simulated flow.
  Continue storing only a hash of the code in the reset record and retain existing attempt throttling.
Replace the browser-hardcoded enrolled-channel confirmation with a server-validated proof that cannot be generated merely by viewing client-side code or knowing an email address.

Ensure reset-token issuance requires an independently authenticated enrolled recovery channel or a server-side simulated channel event that is not directly callable or forgeable by the recovery requester.

Change the MFA design so successful MFA requires proof from a separate enrolled factor/channel rather than returning the valid MFA code to the same browser session that is performing the password reset.
Keep deterministic browser-console test values only in an explicitly isolated demo/testing mode that cannot authorize password resets for real or representative patient accounts.

Replace automatic completeEnrolledChannelEvent authorization with a deterministic mock reset code/token issued for testing, displayed only through the required browser-side console.log/Logs panel after a recovery request.
Add a reset-code/token input form and a dedicated verification endpoint that validates the submitted value against a hashed, session-bound, short-lived, single-use server record.

Replace automatic MFA completion with a separate deterministic mock MFA value, browser-console simulation, and manual MFA-code submission endpoint; require successful MFA validation before allowing password reset.

Ensure the browser cannot learn whether an entered email exists: do not let channel-status, timing, or later UI state differ for known versus unknown identifiers before valid recovery proof is submitted.

Remove or avoid hardcoding a realistic account email identifier in the deployable source; use a clearly non-sensitive test identity supplied through controlled configuration or a test-only deterministic fixture strategy.
Move client executable JavaScript out of the inline <script> element into a same-file server-served route (for example, /app.js) and update CSP to allow only that same-origin script.
Retain the existing CSRF, TLS, rate-limiting, Argon2id, password-policy, secure-cookie, and header controls while updating the recovery flow.
